abstracts.abstract: The exponential growth of IoT devices has fundamentally challenged traditional cloud-centric computing paradigms, creating an urgent need for decentralized architectural frameworks that can handle the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of data sources. This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework called Distributed Edge Intelligence Continuum (DEIC) that reimagines the continuum between edge computing and fog computing as an integrated computational fabric rather than isolated tiers. Unlike conventional approaches that treat edge and fog as hierarchical layers, DEIC introduces a graph-theoretic foundation where computational tasks flow dynamically across device-to-device, device-to-edge, and edge-to-fog connections based on latency constraints and data characteristics. We formalize the problem using Markov Decision Processes with state spaces derived from network topology, computational capacity, and QoS requirements. The theoretical analysis establishes that DEIC achieves optimal task placement with O(n log n) complexity compared to the exponential complexity of brute-force approaches. Furthermore, we prove that the framework converges to a Nash equilibrium under realistic assumptions about device behavior. Simulation results across synthetic and real-world network topologies demonstrate that DEIC reduces end-to-end latency by 47% and improves resource utilization by 34% compared to state-of-the-art hierarchical models. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for designing next-generation distributed systems that natively support the IoT-e-science convergence.

Energy efficiency in cloud data centers remains a critical concern as workload consolidation and dynamic voltage frequency scaling (DVFS) techniques face diminishing returns under heterogeneous workloads. Existing analytical models inadequately capture the complex interactions between virtual machine placement, thermal dynamics, and power consumption in modern virtualized environments. This paper presents an enhanced queueing-network-based analytical model that significantly extends prior work by incorporating thermal coupling effects and non-linear DVFS overheads into the resource management framework. The proposed model introduces a novel state representation that captures the spatial-temporal correlation of server temperatures and their impact on computational efficiency. We derive closed-form expressions for key performance metrics including mean response time, energy consumption, and thermal-aware SLA violation probability. The analytical framework is validated against trace-driven simulations using Google cluster data and PlanetLab measurements. Results indicate that our model predicts energy consumption within 8% of actual measurements, compared to 23% error rates for existing approaches. The derived insights suggest that optimal server utilization thresholds shift from the commonly assumed 70-80% range to 55-65% under thermal-aware provisioning, yielding 18% energy savings without performance degradation.

Scientific workflows in e-science increasingly span distributed computational resources spanning cloud, grid, and edge infrastructure, yet existing workflow management systems treat these environments as separate administrative domains. This paper introduces SciFlow-EdgeCloud, a novel workflow orchestration system that fundamentally reimagines scientific workflow execution as a geo-distributed computing problem rather than a job scheduling problem. SciFlow-EdgeCloud introduces a two-tier architecture where lightweight edge agents perform fine-grained data preprocessing and feature extraction, while cloud-based coordinators handle global workflow optimization and data-intensive aggregation. The system implements a novel data-aware task migration protocol that moves computation to data rather than data to computation, addressing the bandwidth bottlenecks inherent in large-scale scientific datasets. We provide a complete implementation using containerized microservices deployed across AWS, local HPC clusters, and edge nodes equipped with ARM-based processors. Evaluation using real scientific workflows from astronomy (LSST data processing) and genomics (GATK pipelines) demonstrates that SciFlow-EdgeCloud reduces data transfer volumes by 61% and achieves 2.3× speedup compared to traditional cloud-only execution. The system gracefully handles network partitions and edge node mobility through novel checkpointing strategies tailored to workflow structure.

Container orchestration platforms like Kubernetes have become the de facto standard for managing microservice-based applications, yet they lack sophisticated mechanisms for co-optimizing latency-sensitive and throughput-intensive workloads in heterogeneous clusters. Current placement strategies operate reactively, making scheduling decisions based on instantaneous resource availability without considering workload characteristics or future resource demands. This paper presents Latency-Aware Workload Consolidation (LAWC), an enhanced container orchestration system that introduces predictive scheduling through lightweight neural network models trained on historical workload patterns. LAWC augments the Kubernetes scheduler with a novel multi-objective optimization module that jointly optimizes tail latency, resource utilization, and energy consumption. The system introduces adaptive bin-packing algorithms that consider cache hierarchy characteristics and NUMA topology when placing latency-critical containers. We implement LAWC as a set of Kubernetes custom controllers and operators, requiring no modifications to the core scheduler. Evaluation on a 50-node cluster running mixed workloads including web services, stream processing (Apache Kafka), and batch analytics demonstrates that LAWC reduces P99 latency by 35% while improving cluster utilization by 28% compared to default Kubernetes scheduling. The system scales linearly with cluster size and adds less than 2ms overhead to scheduling decisions.
